This file is the refresh-aware implementation behind layer-colour helpers.
applySurface records and refreshes every CGColor it assigns.
The spinner reapplies its shape-layer stroke from draw(_:) on every theme refresh.
The spinner stops before constructing its perpetual animation when Reduce Motion is enabled.

The web page dictates these buttons, not Threading: WKUIDelegate's JavaScript alert, confirm and prompt panels, plus the download-complete offer. None is a decision the app could register or remember, and this file holds no confirmation of its own.
The mark reapplies its shape-layer strokes from draw(_:) on every theme refresh, the same discipline as the spinner.
The mark's core and individually tinted particle fills are reapplied from draw(_:) on every theme refresh beside its strokes.

The draw-in and opt-in particle cadences take named Design.Motion tokens; playDrawIn and pointer entry both return before constructing any animation under Reduce Motion, and particle repetition is removed on pointer exit.

The press animates the mark and does nothing else — the brand names the window rather than opening anything. The rule is right that a view answering a click is usually a control, but the honest fix here is not to subclass ThemedControl: that would give the row a focus ring, an enabled state and an accessibility action for a press that has no effect, which is a worse lie than the one the rule is catching. It stays .staticText carrying the brand's name.
The tiled sidebar pattern is a CGColor by Core Animation's own contract; apply() restates it on every theme change and appearance flip.
The toast's contour rail reapplies its shape-layer stroke from draw(_:) on every theme refresh, the same discipline as the spinner's stroke.
The dwell rail's silhouette is an alpha-only mask; black supplies coverage and carries no theme colour to refresh.

The rail's drain lasts exactly as long as the band's dwell, which is a fact about the clock rather than a motion length — a Design.Motion token here would draw a countdown that disagrees with the timer it depicts. run(for:) returns before constructing any animation under Reduce Motion, which takes the rail away rather than freezing it.

The divider drag stays AppKit's — super runs the whole tracking loop, and the override only reads where it ended. There is no activation to route: the panes it shuts are reachable by keyboard and by the toolbar's own themed controls.

The press is a titlebar's press: it hands the window to performDrag, and a double-click performs the user's own System Settings choice — the gestures NSWindow ran before the takeover theme replaced its frame. Subclassing ThemedControl would give the whole band a focus ring, an enabled state and a press action, none of which a titlebar has; every activation in the band belongs to its buttons, which are real ThemedControls with the full accessibility contract.

The press carries the band sideways and throws it away, which is a notification's swipe rather than an activation: it targets nothing, has no pressed state, and a press that goes nowhere leaves the receipt exactly where it was. Subclassing ThemedControl would give a transient card a focus ring, an enabled state and a press action for a gesture that is none of those. Nothing here is mouse-only, which is the rule's actual concern: the throw does exactly what the band's own ✕ does, and that ✕ is a ThemedIconButton with the full keyboard and accessibility contract, beside the ThemedButton carrying the way back. The mouseDown is also what stops a click falling through a card floating over the very list it reports on.
